extracted.intended_audience: readers/scholars of satire and Renaissance literature; analysts of humor and rhetorical satire
extracted.subtask_description: Extraction of rhetorical targets and recurring satirical motifs from a Renaissance satirical essay (Erasmus' Praise of Folly). The page is a literary/satirical text enumerating types of human folly and methods of comic exposure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Folly's universal beneficence
rubrics_metrics.description: Folly claims to bestow benefits indiscriminately on all people and requires no temples, sacrifices, or priests — 'the whole world is my temple.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The narrator emphasizes that Folly's gifts are given 'readily and indifferently' to everyone, and that public rituals or statues are unnecessary since 'everywhere, as 'tis generally done, men embrace me in their minds, express me in their manners, and represent me in their lives.' This functions as a satirical principle: folly is ubiquitous and social rather than institutional.

rubrics_metrics.name: Worship in behavior over ritual
rubrics_metrics.description: True worship is imitation of virtues rather than external ceremonies — criticism of people who perform outward rites but lack inward virtue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrast: 'How many are there that burn candles to the Virgin Mother... But how few are there that study to imitate her in pureness of life, humility and love of heavenly things, which is the true worship.' Anti-pattern: confusing showy rites with moral substance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Folly among the common people (inventing new follies)
rubrics_metrics.description: The common populace constantly invents new kinds of foolishness and provide endless comic material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The narrator claims the common people 'abound everywhere with so many several sorts of folly' and are a near-constant source of 'sport and pastime' for the gods — a rubric for satire targeting everyday behaviors and trends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Romantic folly (love-sickness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Desperate and unreciprocated passion is a clear mark of folly — the more slighted the lover, the more outrageous his pursuit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'Here's one desperately in love with a young wench, and the more she slights him the more outrageously he loves her.' Satirical target: exaggerated, self-destructive amorous behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Marrying for money
rubrics_metrics.description: Selecting spouses for wealth rather than affection is presented as foolishness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'Another marries a woman's money, not herself.' The text treats mercenary marriages as comic and morally suspect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jealousy and theatrical mourning
rubrics_metrics.description: Excessive jealousy and performative grief are depicted as laughable follies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include 'Another's jealousy keeps more eyes on her than Argos' and 'Another becomes a mourner, and how foolishly he carries it! nay, hires others to bear him company.' The criterion condemns affectation and ostentatious displays of feeling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Idleness and sloth
rubrics_metrics.description: Believing happiness lies in sleep and idleness is counted among follies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicit line: 'Another thinks there is no happiness but in sleep and idleness.' Satirical focus: indolence and pursuit of ease as absurd life goals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meddling in others' affairs
rubrics_metrics.description: Neglecting one's own duties while preoccupying oneself with others' business is foolish.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'Another turmoils himself about other men's business and neglects his own.' This identifies moral and comic fault in distracted self-neglect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Speculative risk for uncertain gain
rubrics_metrics.description: Risking life or safety for a small or doubtful profit is condemned as folly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'Another for a small and uncertain gain exposes his life to the casualties of seas and winds' and 'Another had rather get riches by war than live peaceably at home.' Anti-pattern: reckless pursuit of wealth or glory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Merchant dishonesty and vanity
rubrics_metrics.description: Merchants who engage in dishonest ventures yet claim social honor (gold rings, flattery from friars) are ridiculed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Passage: 'the most foolish and basest of all others are our merchants... who though they lie by no allowance, swear and forswear, steal, cozen, and cheat, yet shuffle themselves into the first rank.' Satirical criterion: hypocrisy and social pretension in commerce.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pedantic grammarians (obsession with minutiae)
rubrics_metrics.description: Grammarians' fixation on trivial linguistic distinctions and their mistreatment of pupils are lampooned as folly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include endless disputes over parts of speech, cruel school discipline, and pride in minute textual discoveries ('as if they had conquered Africa'). They are described as 'ever hunger-starved and slovens... deaf with their noise.' Anti-pattern: valuing pedantic form over useful learning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vanity of obscure erudition
rubrics_metrics.description: Exulting in rare words, worm-eaten manuscripts, or tiny philological finds is portrayed as foolish pride.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: discovery of obscure words 'bubsequa' or 'bovinator' excites 'towerings! what triumphs!' The rubric critiques performative erudition that impresses only a few.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plagiarism and taking other men's glory
rubrics_metrics.description: Passing off others' work as one's own to gain applause is condemned as folly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text: 'they put out other men's works for their own, and transfer that glory which others with great pains have obtained to themselves.' The satirical judgment: temporary applause not worth the dishonor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reciprocal flattery among fools
rubrics_metrics.description: Mutual praising by fools produces inflated self-regard and comic rivalry rather than true merit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'to see them praise one another with reciprocal epistles, verses, and encomiums; fools their fellow fools.' This identifies sycophantic networks as a target of ridicule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advocates' verbosity and legal hair-splitting
rubrics_metrics.description: Lawyers who overwhelm with cases, glosses, and irrelevant learning are mocked as foolish.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Phrase: 'they daily roll Sisyphus his stone, and quote you a thousand cases... heap glosses upon glosses.' Criterion: rhetorical excess and irrelevance in legal argumentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Logicians and sophists (empty prattling)
rubrics_metrics.description: Logicians and sophists who prattle, scold, and lose sense in jargon are lampooned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: They are described as 'a generation of men more prattling than an echo' who 'most obstinately hack and hew one another about a matter of nothing.' Satirical target: rhetorical cleverness without substantive sense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Philosophers' grandiosity and disagreement
rubrics_metrics.description: Philosophers' ambitious claims to knowledge and their internal contradictions reveal folly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Passage: 'they frame in their heads innumerable worlds... and all this too without the least doubting, as if they were Nature's secretaries' but 'they don't agree among themselves.' Criterion: pompous theorizing detached from consensus or reality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scholastic subtleties detached from scripture
rubrics_metrics.description: Theological hair-splitting (terminus a quo/ad quem, transubstantiation timing, etc.) is satirized as excessive and irrelevant compared with apostolic simplicity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: endless disputes over instants, formalities, 'quiddities, haecceities' and whether apostles would have used such doctor-like definitions. The narrator contrasts this with Paul's simpler language, treating scholasticism as comic over-refinement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Creation of paradoxes and sectarian minutiae
rubrics_metrics.description: Invention of paradoxical doctrines and sectarian distinctions (realists, nominalists, Thomists, Occamists, Scotists, etc.) is a mark of folly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text remarks on 'methods of so many Schoolmen' producing entanglements one could not unwind; satirical complaint: multiplying sects and paradoxes for their own sake rather than truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Religious orders' ceremonial obsession vs charity
rubrics_metrics.description: Monks and religious orders who value ceremonies, outward uniformity, and minor rules above charity and true Christian duty are ridiculed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: strict rules about knots of shoes, habit fabric and color, hours of sleep, bushels wide cowl — 'how disproportionate it is' and 'they do not endeavor how they may be like Christ, but how they may differ among themselves.' Satirical principle: external observance without inward virtue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypocrisy of begging friars and abuse of confession
rubrics_metrics.description: Friars who flatter the rich, exploit confessions for information, and beg under cover of religion are lampooned as morally corrupt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Passage: 'they flatter themselves... they are privy to all men's secrets by means of confessions' and may 'revenge themselves in their public sermons' — target: clerical hypocrisy and venality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theatrical preaching and rhetorical tricks
rubrics_metrics.description: Preachers who use showy gestures, voice shifts, borrowed fables, and rhetorical posturing to impress rather than instruct are satirized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'Good God! what several postures they have! How they shift their voice, sing out their words, skip up and down, and are ever and anon making such new faces' and the mixing of unrelated sources (poets, Nile, zodiac) into sermons. Anti-pattern: style substituting for substance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Over-systematization of religious practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Counting religious merit by the number of ceremonies, fasts, prayers, or externally measurable feats rather than moral qualities is criticized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: boastful lists — 'a large trough full of all kinds of fish; another tumble you out so many bushels of prayers; another reckon you so many myriads of fasts' — with the narrator expecting Christ would ask where charity is. Satirical rubric: quantifying piety is empty.
